strengths: Genuinely novel and well-motivated research question: connecting classical polynomial reducibility from computational complexity theory to pretraining/transfer decisions for neural CO solvers is an original framing, and the paper is careful and honest that this relationship is non-trivial and only partially established.

Careful and thorough experimental design in the pairwise transferability study: the progression from frozen-backbone transfer, to weight inversion initialization, to full fine-tuning, to graph-transformer global message passing, to implementing the 'true' reduction via the complement graph (Table 4, Exp #4-11) systematically isolates what matters, and the analysis of why frozen representations fail under distribution shift is insightful.

Useful methodological contributions in their own right: the Hamiltonian-based MaxClique loss improves state of the art on RB-small over Wenkel et al. (2025) with an identical architecture, the ablation confirming the loss formulation (not the architecture) drives the gain, and the parallelized k-seed decoder fixing the runtime bottleneck of prior work.

Interesting leave-one-out multi-task findings (Sec. 5.1, Table 5), e.g., that having one reducibly-related task in the pretraining set suffices for rapid transfer while redundant related tasks can hurt, gives actionable guidance for pretraining-set selection.
Open-source implementation is promised, and the paper includes detailed appendices on problem formulations and related work that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to very small synthetic graphs (RB-small with ~200 nodes and BA-small). For a paper whose stated ambition is 'stepping stone towards foundation models for neural CO', there is no evidence at any realistic scale, no real-world graph datasets, and no larger benchmarks (e.g., SATLIB, TSPLib-scale instances), making the foundation-model framing speculative.

The central hypothesis receives only partially positive support: in the flagship MIS/MVC -> MaxClique experiments, most transfer settings 'fall significantly short of the baselines' (Table 4), and even the best fine-tuned result requires substantial fine-tuning. The honest negative/ambiguous results are valuable, but they mean the paper's contribution is an exploratory study rather than a demonstrated technique.

The theoretical connection is informal throughout. There is no formal characterization of when a polynomial reduction between problems implies (or fails to imply) representation transferability, so the link to 'computational reducibility' remains largely a narrative device guiding experiment design; the paper itself concedes further work is needed.

Baselines are limited: comparisons are restricted to a handful of unsupervised SSL-GNN variants and GFN; no comparison against recent multi-task/generalist CO solvers (UniCO, GOAL, RL-based pretrained solvers) that represent the actual competing paradigm for unified CO models.

Statistical support is thin: 3-5 seeds per configuration, some tables with large variances (e.g., Coloring in Table 7, leave-one-out MDS in Table 5), and several conclusions rest on differences within or barely exceeding noise.
There is no explicit limitations section, despite the results being preliminary by the authors' own admission; the caveats are scattered through the text rather than consolidated.

Some findings are unsurprising (MIS<->MVC transfer trivially works because the problems are complements on identical graph topology), which weakens the novelty of the strongest positive results; the genuinely novel transfer cases are the ones where the method underperforms baselines.

strengths: The research question — whether computational reducibility can inform transfer learning for neural combinatorial optimization — is interesting and underexplored, and framing pretraining task selection via the polynomial reduction literature (Karp reductions, Filar et al.'s linear orbits) is a novel and thought-provoking angle.

The pairwise transferability study (Sec. 4) is carefully designed, with sensible ablations distinguishing frozen vs. fine-tuned backbones, node-feature distribution shifts between G and its complement, and the inclusion of a graph-transformer stack to test whether global message passing helps adapt to topology shifts.

The GCON + Ising/Hamiltonian loss combination attains a new state-of-the-art result for MaxClique on RB-small (16.92 vs. 15.87 in Wenkel et al., 2025), and the paper includes a useful controlled comparison showing the Hamiltonian loss outperforms a Motzkin-Straus-style quadratic variant (18.04 vs. 15.5 MIS size).
The parallelized construction of k seed sets in the sequential decoder is a practical improvement over Wenkel et al. (2025), enabling larger k at much lower runtime.
The paper is largely honest that the reducibility–transferability connection is 'not trivial' and that many transfer settings fall short of from-scratch baselines, which is commendable candor.
weaknesses: The central claim is only weakly supported. The abstract and conclusion claim a 'strong evidence of transfer' and a stepping stone toward foundation models, but the empirical evidence largely shows the opposite for most task pairs: in Table 4, nearly all fine-tuning settings fall short of the from-scratch baseline, and in Table 5 the fine-tuning gains are marginal (MaxClique 4.32 vs. 4.31, MIS 111.56 vs. 111.33) or negative (MDS 36.15 vs. 35.57). Only MaxCut and K-coloring show meaningful benefit, which undercuts the headline framing.

The evaluation is limited to very small synthetic graphs (RB-small and BA-small). No real-world or larger benchmark graphs are used, and on RB-small Gurobi substantially outperforms all learned methods (e.g., 19.05 vs. 211.69 for MVC), so practical significance is unclear. Claims about 'foundation models' for CO are a substantial overreach from ~3-run experiments on small random graphs.

The reducibility→transferability thesis is examined seriously only for the trivial MIS/MVC/MaxClique reductions; the multi-task section (Sec. 5) is essentially standard multi-task pretraining/fine-tuning, and the pretraining set selection in Sec. 5.2 is justified largely by ad-hoc observations (e.g., Table 6) rather than by the reduction theory, so the theory–practice link the title promises remains mostly anecdotal.

No empirical comparison against existing multi-task/generalist neural CO solvers (GOAL, UniCO, Li et al., Wang et al., etc.) — these are discussed in related work but never run as baselines, making it impossible to judge whether the reduction-informed pretraining strategy is actually better than generic multi-task pretraining or simpler task-similarity heuristics.

Statistical rigor is thin: 3–5 runs per setting, high variance in several results (e.g., coloring baseline 49.04 ± 21.84, GT setting #9 std 0.63 with the text noting one lucky run at 16.75), and several conclusions rest on differences within error bars.

Presentation and consistency problems: the open-source URL promised in the abstract is missing; the text in Sec. 4.2 references experiments #12–#13 that do not exist in Table 4 (which has only 11 rows); typos throughout ('incresingly', 'a a common', 'singe task models'); Table 3 baseline MVC (211.69) is labeled as the value being improved in Table 2 while transferred models slightly beat it, which deserves more scrutiny than it receives.
There is no explicit limitations section discussing the small-graph regime, the negative results in Table 4, or the gap to exact solvers, despite the conclusions making broad forward-looking claims.

The leave-one-out 'almost always leads to faster convergence' claim (abstract) is supported only at 20 epochs on BA-small graphs with a frozen-then-unfrozen protocol; no wall-clock or FLOP accounting is given, so 'faster' is only in epochs and is not compared to simply training the single task with an equivalent compute budget.

strengths: Novel and intellectually appealing framing: connecting classical polynomial-reducibility knowledge from theoretical CS to pretraining/transfer decisions for neural CO solvers is a fresh angle that most multi-task CO works (GOAL, UniCO, RL-based approaches) do not explore.

The pairwise transferability study (Sec. 4) is well designed and informative, including instructive negative results: frozen backbones fail under complement-graph distribution shift, output-head inversion alone cannot close the duality gap, and implementing the 'true' reduction (solving MIS on G-bar) with full fine-tuning matches the baseline in a third of the epochs.

The ablation in Table 2 and the analysis of Hamiltonian vs. Motzkin-Straus losses (Sec. 3.4/4) is a useful empirical contribution, showing a new state-of-the-art MaxClique result on RB-small and demonstrating that loss formulation choice materially changes results despite similar architectures.

The multi-task experiments (leave-one-out, Table 5-7) are honest and include non-trivial conclusions, e.g., that one reducible task in the pretraining set suffices for rapid transfer, and that MDS benefits from excluding MaxCut/MVC from co-pretraining.

The paper is candid that the reducibility-transferability connection is 'not trivial' and positions the work as a stepping stone rather than overclaiming a solved problem; an open-source implementation is provided.
weaknesses: The central thesis—that computational reducibility leads to/informs transferability—is only weakly supported by the evidence. The clearest transfer gains occur for MaxCut and K-coloring, and K-coloring is explicitly noted as NOT linearly reducible to the other tasks; conversely, reducible pairs (e.g., MaxClique) show marginal or negligible gains (Table 5: 4.31 vs 4.32). The practical pretraining-set selection (MDS-MIS-Coloring) actually deviates from the reduction structure, so the reduction narrative functions more as motivation than as a validated predictor.

Experimental scale is very limited: only small synthetic datasets (RB-small, BA-small), no real-world or large graphs, and no transfer tests to unseen graph distributions. This significantly weakens the ambitious 'foundation model for neural CO' claims in the abstract and conclusion.

No comparison against existing unified/multi-task CO baselines (e.g., GOAL, UniCO, Guo et al. 2025) in the transfer setting, so the practical value of the proposed pipeline relative to prior unified solvers is unknown.

Statistical rigor is thin: only 3-5 runs per setting, no significance tests, and several reported differences are within or near noise (e.g., Table 5 MaxClique, Table 3 MVC). Table 2 baselines (Gurobi, GFN) lack error bars.

Internal inconsistencies and polish issues: the text in Sec. 4.2 refers to rows '#12' and '#13' but Table 4 contains only 11 rows; the promised open-source link is blank; typos ('incresingly', 'follow a a common', 'singe task models').

Methodological novelty is limited: the backbone (GCON, Wenkel et al. 2025) and losses (Ising Hamiltonians, Lucas 2014 / Sanokowski et al. 2024) are adopted from prior work; the contribution is primarily the transfer study, which increases the importance of the above evidence limitations.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the main text: hyperparameters, A/B penalty ratios, k seeds, and dataset generation procedures are not specified (appendices only cover problem definitions and related work), making independent verification difficult despite the promised code release.

strengths: The central question—whether complexity-theoretic polynomial reductions can inform transferability of neural CO solvers—is genuinely novel and well-motivated, connecting two literatures that rarely interact. The framing as a 'stepping stone' rather than overclaiming a full foundation model is honest.

The pairwise transferability study (Sec. 4) is carefully designed to disentangle the effect of topology-preserving vs. topology-altering reductions (MIS↔MVC vs. MIS↔MaxClique via complement graphs), with sensible experimental variants (frozen backbone, head inversion, graph transformer layers, implementing the true reduction on the complement graph). The nuanced findings—e.g., that theoretical equivalence alone is insufficient and fine-tuning is needed to close the distribution shift—are informative.

Appendix C provides a valuable and arguably underpublicized contribution: a direct comparison of multi-task learning against a 'unified-task' reduction-based framework (MDS-based), quantifying the node/edge blow-up from chained reductions (up to ~123x) and showing that distribution shift from reductions causes negative transfer at scale (Table 10). This analysis goes beyond the main experiments.

The leave-one-out multi-task analysis (Sec. 5.1, Fig. 2) yields a clean, actionable insight: transfer succeeds if at least one reducible task is in the pretraining set, and this guides a principled (if heuristic) pretraining-set selection in Sec. 5.2.

Additional experiments strengthen the work: size extrapolation (Table 12), timing comparisons (Tables 13-14), and zero-shot transfer to out-of-distribution DIMACS instances (Table 15) demonstrating that pretrained representations beat random initialization on real hard instances.

The paper is transparent about limitations: negative results (frozen backbones fail across topology shifts, MDS shows no benefit from transfer, most fine-tuned MaxClique settings fall short of baselines) are reported clearly, and open-source code is promised.
weaknesses: The scale and diversity of evaluation is limited. All main experiments use small synthetic graphs (RB and BA families, 200-1200 nodes) with a tiny 39.2K-parameter backbone. Claims about 'foundation models for neural CO' are thus quite extrapolated; only a zero-shot DIMACS probe touches real-world instances. No comparison against existing generalist/multi-task CO solvers (GOAL, UniCO, or the SAT-based methods discussed) is performed on the transfer benchmarks, making it hard to gauge the practical value of the proposed pretraining-set selection.

Some headline conclusions rest on differences within or near reported standard deviations with few runs (3-5). For example, in Table 5 MaxClique 'improves' from 4.31 to 4.32, MDS fine-tuning is actually slightly worse (36.15 vs 35.57), and in Table 7 several fine-tuned vs. baseline gaps are small relative to variance. The claim of 'avoiding negative transfer' is contradicted in at least one cell. More runs and significance testing would materially strengthen the evidence.

The link between reducibility and transferability remains largely correlational. There is no analysis of what the shared representations contain (the paper only 'conjectures' that MIS representations suffice for MVC), no probing or similarity metrics, and the pretraining-set selection in Sec. 5.2 mixes reducibility arguments with heuristic observations (e.g., the single Table 6 observation driving exclusion of MaxCut/MVC), so it is unclear how much of the success is attributable to the theory-guided recipe vs. generic multi-task pretraining.

Performance gaps to optimal remain sizable (e.g., MaxClique 16.92 vs. true 19.07 on RB-small; Gurobi and even GFN outperform on MIS), and the transfer benefit is primarily convergence speed in a low-resource regime rather than final solution quality, which limits practical significance.

Presentation issues: numerous typos ('incresingly', 'transfering', 'standart', 'We follow a a common architectural design'), a broken/missing URL in the abstract, Table 2's formatting is confusing (Gurobi results appear misaligned across columns), and Figure 2 is small and hard to read. These do not obscure the science but indicate a rushed manuscript.

strengths: The central question — whether polynomial-time reducibility among CO problems can guide transfer/pretraining decisions — is genuinely interesting and offers a fresh angle relative to prior multi-task neural CO work (GOAL, UniCO, SAT-based approaches), which mostly selects pretraining tasks heuristically.

The paper is unusually honest about negative and partial results: frozen backbones fail under topology-shifting reductions (Sec. 4.2), most fine-tuned models fall short of from-scratch baselines (Table 4), and MDS shows no fine-tuning benefit (Table 5). The authors explicitly state that the reducibility–transferability connection 'is not trivial' rather than overselling it.

Appendix C is a valuable addition: the controlled comparison against a unified-task (MDS-reduction) framework (Tables 9–10), with quantified graph blow-ups (122× node growth for chained MaxClique→MDS reductions), gives concrete, actionable insight into why structure-altering reductions harm transfer — arguably the most informative part of the paper.

The empirical scope is broad for an initial study: pairwise transfer (Sec. 4), leave-one-out multi-task transfer (Sec. 5.1), a reasoned pretraining-set selection validated in Sec. 5.2 and on BA-large graphs, size extrapolation, inference timing, and zero-shot evaluation on DIMACS instances (Table 15), all with an open-source implementation.
The improved Hamiltonian-based losses yield a meaningful gain over Wenkel et al. (2025) on MaxClique (16.92 vs 15.87), with a sensible ablation supporting the loss-function choice.
weaknesses: The central claim — that reducibility knowledge informs transferability — is only weakly supported, and the evidence is largely consistent with mundane similarity effects. The only reductions actually exploited are the textbook MIS↔MVC↔MaxClique complementarity relations (Lemma 2.1); the celebrated 'linear orbit' results of Filar et al. (2019) are cited but never operationalized. The experiments show that (i) tasks with trivially complementary solutions transfer, and (ii) tasks without structural overlap do not — conclusions that do not require polynomial-reduction theory to anticipate. No reduction from the theory that is not already 'trivial' is ever shown to yield transfer, so the paper's framing significantly outruns its results.

The empirical gains of the final pipeline are modest and uneven. In Table 7, fine-tuning beats the 20-epoch baseline for all tasks but is on par with (or worse than) the full 200-epoch single-task baseline for MaxCut, MaxClique, MIS, and MVC; only MDS and Coloring show clear full-training gains. Table 3 shows frozen-backbone transfer never matches the from-scratch baseline, and in Table 4 the majority of transfer settings underperform their baselines. The 'important step towards foundational models' narrative is not warranted by these effect sizes.

Scale and statistical rigor are limited for an ICML main-track paper: everything is on synthetic RB/BA graphs with 200–300 (and 800–1200) nodes; RB-small results use 3 runs; the backbone is tiny (39.2K parameters); and there is no comparison against existing multi-task solvers (GOAL, UniCO, Li et al., Wang et al.) on a shared benchmark, so it is impossible to judge whether the proposed framework is competitive, only that it beats its own weak from-scratch ablations.

The paper contains presentational and consistency defects that undermine confidence: Table 4 is referenced with rows #12 and #13 that do not exist (the table ends at #11); the abstract's repository URL is missing; there are typos ('incresingly', 'singe task', 'transfering', 'standart'); and citations dated 2025/2026 (e.g., Feng et al., 2026; Wenkel et al., 2025) suggest incomplete proofreading.

There is no theory or even formalized hypothesis connecting complexity-bounded reductions to transferability; the link is asserted narratively ('stepping stone', 'in the spirit of'). Key confounds — node-feature overlap, loss-function similarity, and decoder sharing — are not disentangled from the reduction structure, so the causal role of reducibility remains unestablished. A controls study (e.g., transfer between structurally similar but reduction-unrelated tasks) is absent.

Limitations are not consolidated or candidly scoped: nowhere does the paper acknowledge that only six NP-hard tasks, one architecture family, and synthetic graph families were considered, that coloring results are erratic (violations of 61.92±36.11 in Table 5; +71.26% degradation in Table 12), or that the method was not validated against any external multi-task baseline. The Impact Statement is boilerplate.

strengths: Original and interesting research question: connecting computational reducibility from theoretical CS to transfer learning for neural CO is a fresh angle, and the paper is candid that the connection 'is not trivial and further work is needed' rather than overclaiming a theory-informed recipe.

Well-structured empirical investigation: pairwise transfer (MIS↔MVC, MIS/MVC↔MaxClique) with clear experimental questions (frozen vs. fine-tuned, global message-passing, implementing the 'true' reduction), followed by leave-one-out multi-task transfer and a pretraining-set selection study. The ablations (Table 4) are thoughtfully designed, e.g., isolating the effect of complement-graph features and graph transformers.

Useful negative and nuanced findings: frozen backbones fail under topology shift (complement graphs), linear-head transfer cannot close the duality gap, and Appendix C convincingly shows that chained reductions (MaxClique → MDS with ~100x graph blow-up) cause negative transfer while the proposed multi-task alternative succeeds. This is a genuinely informative contribution for the community.

Good reproducibility posture: open-source code promised, architecture/hyperparameters fully specified (Table 8), run counts and hardware stated, and additional results on large graphs, size extrapolation, timing, and zero-shot DIMACS evaluation provided.

The GCON-based solver itself is competitive (Table 2), improving over prior GCON results on MaxClique due to a better Hamiltonian loss, which lends credibility to the baselines used in the transfer studies.
weaknesses: The central 'reducibility-informed transfer' claim is supported only informally. No theoretical or even semi-formal connection is established between polynomial reductions and representation transfer; the actual reductions used in experiments are the trivial complement-based identities (Lemma 2.1), and the deeper result (Filar et al. linear orbit) is used only qualitatively to justify the pretraining set. The pretraining set choice in Sec. 5.2 (MDS-MIS-Coloring) is assembled from post-hoc observations (Tables 5-6) rather than from the reducibility structure, which undercuts the headline motivation.

Evidence of transfer benefit is sometimes thin. In Table 5, several fine-tuning gains are marginal and possibly within noise (MaxClique 4.32 vs 4.31; MIS 111.56 vs 111.33; MDS actually worsens 36.15 vs 35.57), yet the abstract claims pretraining 'almost always leads to faster convergence... while avoiding negative transfer.' Only 3-5 runs are reported with no significance testing. The coloring comparison (fine-tuned 24.19±9.08 vs FULL 3.52±1.52) shows the proposed approach remains far behind full training on that task.

Limited scale and dataset diversity: all controlled experiments are on small synthetic graphs (RB-small 200-300 nodes; BA graphs up to 1200 nodes). Real-world evaluation is only zero-shot inference on DIMACS instances with no fine-tuning and large gaps to best-known solutions, so practical significance beyond synthetic regimes remains unproven.

No empirical comparison to existing multi-task/generalist CO solvers (GOAL, UniCO, Li et al., Wang et al.) — these are discussed in related work but the proposed framework is evaluated only against its own single-task baselines, making it hard to gauge whether the reducibility-informed design adds value over generic multi-task pretraining.

Presentation issues that should be fixed: Table 4 analysis references '#12' and '#13' which do not exist in the table (should be #10/#11); several typos ('incresingly', 'a a', 'singe task models', 'standart', 'transfering'); Table 2 does not include the GCON value for MIS highlighted consistently with the stated gold/silver scheme; the leave-one-out claim of 'strong evidence of transfer' overstates what the small deltas in Table 5 support.

The reduction in Appendix C (Algorithm 1) is stated without proof of correctness (e.g., the role of degree-0 node removal is not justified), and the claimed equivalence 'The MVC on G is thus equivalent to the MDS on G′' is asserted without derivation.
